literal: Xuan, styled Shijian, when entering the passes was seven years old.
idiomatic: Xuan, styled Shijian, was seven when he entered the passes.

literal: In Qi he served as Court Gentleman for the Dynasty and Magistrate of Chengping.
idiomatic: In Qi he was Court Gentleman and Magistrate of Chengping.

literal: When Qi fell, Emperor Wu of Zhou saw Xuan, treated him with special encouragement, and at once made him Chief Superior Gentleman of the Earth Office.
idiomatic: Qi's fall brought special favor; he became Chief Superior Gentleman of the Earth Office.

literal: At the end of the Elephant era he was Internal Military Staff Officer to Chancellor Wen of Sui.
idiomatic: At Elephant's end he was staff officer to Sui's chancellor.

literal: Xuan's younger brother Rong, styled Shiqing, was the most famous; in youth he held prominent posts.
idiomatic: Younger Rong, styled Shiqing, was most famed and rose young.

literal: At the end of the Elephant era he reached the rank of Grand General and Duke of Dingling.
idiomatic: By Elephant's end he was Grand General and Duke of Dingling.

literal: His younger brother Li from youth was loyal and careful, attending at the emperor's side; Taiwu was especially intimate with him.
idiomatic: Younger Li, loyal from youth, attended Taiwu closely.

literal: His conduct was cautious; at first he had no fault.
idiomatic: He was careful and faultless at first.

literal: Enfeoffed as Viscount of Zhang'an, he was gradually promoted to Minister of the Southern Court.
idiomatic: Made Viscount of Zhang'an, he rose to Minister of the Southern Court.

literal: When Taiwu died, Prince of Nan'an Yu was enthroned.
idiomatic: Taiwu died; Prince Yu of Nan'an took the throne.

literal: Soon he was killed by the eunuch Zong Ai and others.
idiomatic: Soon eunuch Zong Ai and others killed him.

literal: The hundred officials were anxious and knew not whom to enthrone.
idiomatic: Officials panicked, unsure whom to enthrone.

literal: Li was first to propose the great plan; with Palace Director Changsun Kehou, Minister Yuan He, and Feathered Forest Cadet Liu Ni he welcomed Emperor Wencheng from the park and enthroned him.
idiomatic: Li led the plan with Kehou, Yuan He, and Liu Ni to raise Wencheng from the park.

literal: The altars were secured—Li's stratagem.
idiomatic: The realm was saved by Li's plot.

literal: Hence he received trust at the heart; among those at court none surpassed him.
idiomatic: He won the emperor's core trust; none at court matched him.

literal: At the beginning of Xing'an he was enfeoffed Prince of Pingyuan.
idiomatic: At Xing'an he was made Prince of Pingyuan.

literal: Li repeatedly declined and was not heard; he then memorialized to yield to his father.
idiomatic: He declined again and again, then asked to yield to his father.

literal: Wencheng said: "I am lord of all under Heaven—can I not enfeoff father and son as two princes?"
idiomatic: Wencheng said, "Can I not make father and son both princes?"

literal: His father Si was made Prince of Dongping.
idiomatic: His father Si became Prince of Dongping.

literal: Li was soon moved to Attendant, General Who Pacifies the Army, and Duke of the Masses; his descendants were restored, and titles were granted his wife and consorts.
idiomatic: Soon Attendant, Pacifying-Army General, Duke of the Masses; kin restored, consorts titled.

literal: Because favor came again and again, he firmly declined and would not accept; the emperor esteemed him the more.
idiomatic: Repeated honors he refused; the emperor esteemed him more.

literal: He held the post of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
idiomatic: He was Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.

literal: Li loved learning and cherished scholars; he constantly made lecturing his occupation.
idiomatic: He loved scholars and lectured constantly.

literal: He was very filial; on his father's death his mourning waste exceeded the rites.
idiomatic: Filial to excess, his father's mourning broke the rites.

literal: In the sixth year of Heping, Wencheng died.
idiomatic: Heping 6, Wencheng died.

literal: Earlier Li had been treating illness at the hot springs in Dai Commandery; hearing the calamity he wished to hurry back.
idiomatic: He was at Dai's hot springs when news came; he raced to return.

literal: Those about him stopped him, saying: "The imperial carriage has just halted; your virtue and fame have long been weighty—if wicked ministers should envy your repute, there may be unforeseen disaster."
idiomatic: Attendants warned, "The throne is empty; your fame may draw traitors."

literal: Li said: "How could one hear of a lord and father's death and still weigh the risk of calamity!"
idiomatic: Li said, "Shall I fear trouble at my father's death?"

literal: He galloped back at once.
idiomatic: He galloped back.

literal: Earlier, Yifu Hun was arrogant and repeatedly did what was unlawful; Li often remonstrated and therefore was hated and killed.
idiomatic: Yifu Hun's arrogance drew Li's remonstrance; Hun killed him.

literal: Posthumous name Prince Jian; buried with honor at Jinling.
idiomatic: Posthumous name Jian; buried at Jinling.

literal: Emperor Xiaowen, recording former-court merit, paired Li in the temple hall.
idiomatic: Xiaowen paired him in the ancestral temple.

literal: Li had two wives: the elder was the Du clan, the second the Zhang clan.
idiomatic: Two wives: Du, then Zhang.

literal: The eldest son Dingguo was born of the Du clan;
idiomatic: Eldest Dingguo was Du's son;

literal: the second, Rui, was born of the Zhang clan.
idiomatic: second Rui was Zhang's.

literal: His son Xinzhi, styled Qingshi, had bearing elegant and correct.
idiomatic: Son Xinzhi, styled Qingshi, was grave and elegant.

literal: He inherited the title; by regulation it was reduced to duke.
idiomatic: He inherited, reduced to duke by rule.

literal: He married Emperor Xianwen's daughter Princess of Changshan and was made Commandant of the Horse Guards and Regular Attendant Direct.
idiomatic: He married Princess Changshan, became Horse Guards Commandant and Regular Attendant.

literal: In the Jingming era, because of cousin Xiu's crime, he was dismissed.
idiomatic: Jingming: cousin Xiu's crime cost him office.

literal: Soon, as the emperor's son-in-law, he was again made Regular Attendant Direct and Unimpeded.
idiomatic: Soon restored as the emperor's son-in-law.

literal: He served as Governor of Yan and Qing in succession, both with political achievement.
idiomatic: He governed Yan and Qing with merit.

literal: Transferred to General Who Pacifies the North and Governor of Xiang.
idiomatic: Made Pacifying-North General and Governor of Xiang.

literal: At death posthumously General Who Pacifies the East and Governor of Ji, posthumous name Hui.
idiomatic: At death posthumously Pacifying-East General and Governor of Ji, posthumous name Hui.

literal: Earlier Dingguo married a woman of the Liu clan of Hedong and had a son Anbao.
idiomatic: Dingguo married Liu of Hedong and had Anbao.

literal: Later he married a daughter of Lu Dushi of Fanyang and had Xinzhi.
idiomatic: Later he married Lu Dushi's daughter and had Xinzhi.

literal: Both households were old families, yet legitimate wife and concubine were not distinguished.
idiomatic: Both were great houses, but wife and concubine were not ranked.

literal: After Dingguo died, the two sons contended for their father's title.
idiomatic: After Dingguo's death the sons fought for the title.

literal: Vice Director Li Chong was favored at the time and was allied by marriage with Dushi's son Boyuan.
idiomatic: Vice Director Li Chong favored Boyuan, Lu Dushi's son-in-law.

literal: Chong therefore sided with him, and Xinzhi thereby inherited the title, married the princess, and his posts blazed with glory.
idiomatic: Chong backed Boyuan's side; Xinzhi took the title, the princess, and glory.

literal: Anbao sank into poverty and could not escape cold and hunger.
idiomatic: Anbao fell to poverty and hunger.

literal: Xinzhi's bearing was gentle and careful; Xiaowen, as his son-in-law, showed him special intimacy.
idiomatic: Gentle Xinzhi won Xiaowen's special favor as son-in-law.

literal: In the Xuanwu era, before forty, he repeatedly governed the three frontiers—the age counted it glory.
idiomatic: Before forty in Xuanwu's time he held three frontiers—a glory of the age.

literal: After Xinzhi died, his mother Lu grieved until grief killed her.
idiomatic: Mother Lu mourned him to death.

literal: The princess served her mother-in-law with a filial name.
idiomatic: The princess was famed for serving her mother-in-law.

literal: At the beginning of Shengui she and Princess of Langye of the Mu clan were both made Female Attendants.
idiomatic: Shengui's start made her and Mu's Langye princess Female Attendants.

literal: She was also free of jealousy; because Xinzhi had no sons, she took concubines for him, yet all bore daughters.
idiomatic: Without jealousy she took concubines; all bore daughters.

literal: The princess had three daughters and no sons; she took Xinzhi's cousin Xidao's fourth son Zizhang as heir.
idiomatic: Three daughters, no son—she adopted cousin Xidao's fourth son Zizhang.

literal: Zizhang, styled Mingyuan, original name Shishen.
idiomatic: Zizhang, styled Mingyuan, born Shishen.

literal: At sixteen he left his birth house; toward the princess he fulfilled every rite.
idiomatic: At sixteen he entered her house and observed every rite.

literal: Chancellor Prince Yong of Gaoyang often said: "Though Princess Changshan has no son, taking Zizhang as son surpasses bearing one's own."
idiomatic: Prince Yong of Gaoyang said, "Adopting Zizhang beats a son of her own."

literal: In the Zhenguang era he inherited the title Duke of Dongjun and rose to Attendant of the Yellow Gate.
idiomatic: Zhenguang: he inherited Duke of Dongjun and rose to Yellow Gate Attendant.

literal: Zizhang's wife was the daughter of Prince of Xianyang Xi.
idiomatic: His wife was Prince Xi's daughter.

literal: When Xi was executed, she was raised in Prince of Pengcheng's mansion; Emperor Zhuangdi cherished her like his own sisters.
idiomatic: Xi died; she was raised with Pengcheng's daughters, cherished by Zhuangdi.

literal: At the beginning of Jianyi, Erzhu Rong wished to follow old precedent and enfeoff commoners as princes; thus Zizhang was made Prince of Puyang.
idiomatic: Jianyi: Rong enfeoffed commoners; Zizhang became Prince of Puyang.

literal: Soon an edict revoked it; he returned to his former title.
idiomatic: Soon the edict was revoked.

literal: In the Tianping era he was made Guard General and Governor of Ying; he left office for his mother's mourning.
idiomatic: Tianping: Guard General and Governor of Ying; he mourned his mother.

literal: In the Yuanxiang era, with his existing general's title he was made Governor of Qi, then also General of Agile Cavalry acting for Huai, then Governor of Northern Yu, then Governor of Xu—all generals' titles as before.
idiomatic: Yuanxiang: Qi, Agile Cavalry at Huai, Northern Yu, Xu—three provinces in a year.

literal: One year, three provinces—the age counted it glory.
idiomatic: Three provinces in one year was glory.

literal: Returning to court, he was made Guard Grand General and Senior Grand Master of the Splendid, acting for Ying.
idiomatic: At court: Guard Grand General, Senior Splendid Master, acting Ying.

literal: Soon Attendant, again acting for Cang.
idiomatic: Soon Attendant, acting Cang.

literal: Advanced in title to General of Agile Cavalry.
idiomatic: Promoted to Agile Cavalry General.

literal: Acting for Ji.
idiomatic: Acting Ji.

literal: Made Lecturer, concurrently Minister of the Seven Armies, acting for Qing.
idiomatic: Lecturer, Seven Armies Minister, acting Qing.

literal: When Zizhang first held provinces he was grasping; in later years he reformed, and from Qing, Ji, Cang, and Ying he had great contemporary praise.
idiomatic: Early greed gave way to reform; Qing, Ji, Cang, and Ying won praise.

literal: He also received others with empty humility; gentlemen revered and loved him.
idiomatic: Humble toward others, he was loved by gentlemen.

literal: Made Director of the Secretariat.
idiomatic: Director of the Secretariat.

literal: At death posthumously Commissioner with credentials equal to the Three Excellencies, posthumous name Wensuan.
idiomatic: At death posthumously Commissioner, posthumous name Wensuan.

literal: Zizhang deeply loved Daoist arts; once gravely ill, his medicine needed praying mantis egg-cases.
idiomatic: He loved Daoism; grave illness needed mantis egg-cases in medicine.

literal: Zizhang could not bear to harm living things and therefore did not take the medicine—such was his benevolence.
idiomatic: He would not harm creatures and refused the dose—such was his kindness.

literal: He taught six sons with elegant discipline.
idiomatic: He trained six sons with strict grace.

literal: His son Yang.
idiomatic: His son Yang.

literal: Yang, styled Yunju, was clever from youth with fine spirit.
idiomatic: Yang, styled Yunju, was quick and fine-spirited.

literal: He loved learning without tiring, read widely, and penetrated the great meaning of the Five Classics.
idiomatic: He read widely and grasped the Five Classics.

literal: Skilled at composition, he was greatly prized by Xing Shao of Hejian.
idiomatic: Xing Shao of Hejian prized his writing.

literal: Shao also befriended Zizhang and once told him: "From your old oyster I drew forth a pearl—shall I have the crowd bow to the chronicle?"
idiomatic: Shao told Zizhang, "From your oyster came a pearl—shall I have men bow to the chronicle?"

literal: Hence his fame rose daily and gentlemen of the girdle praised him.
idiomatic: Fame rose; gentry praised him.

literal: He began as Supernumerary Regular Attendant, then Secretariat Chief Clerk to Grand General Wenxiang, Secretariat Attendant, concurrent Secretariat Vice Director, and in his existing office concurrently Junior Mentor of the Heir Apparent.
idiomatic: He rose from attendant to Wenxiang's clerk, Secretariat posts, and Junior Mentor.

literal: From Liang and Wei exchanging envoys each year, Yang often jointly received banquets.
idiomatic: When Liang and Wei exchanged envoys, Yang often hosted banquets.

literal: At the feast composing poems, Yang always finished first; though not fully polished, he was praised for speed.
idiomatic: At feasts he finished poems first—praised for speed if not polish.

literal: Made Secretariat Vice Director and edited the national history.
idiomatic: Secretariat Vice Director editing national history.

literal: He left office for his father's mourning.
idiomatic: He mourned his father.

literal: In mourning he fulfilled every rite; grief wasted him to bone; an edict recalled him in his existing office.
idiomatic: Mourning broke his body; edict recalled him.

literal: When Grand General Wenxiang was stationed at Ye, he prized this utmost conduct and came in person to his gate to comfort him.
idiomatic: Wenxiang at Ye came himself to comfort him.

literal: Yang's mother was Princess of Shangyong of Wei.
idiomatic: His mother was Wei's Princess of Shangyong.

literal: First enfeoffed as Princess of Lantian—a woman of high clarity.
idiomatic: First Princess of Lantian—a woman of clarity.

literal: She had great resolve.
idiomatic: She had strong resolve.

literal: Yang's six brothers were all born of the princess; therefore Xing Shao often told people: "Lantian bears jade—indeed not empty praise."
idiomatic: Six brothers all her sons—Shao said, "Lantian bears jade—not empty fame."

literal: The princess taught her sons all by righteous rule.
idiomatic: She taught her sons righteousness.

literal: Though the wound was vast and grief deep, springing from inborn nature;
idiomatic: Grief vast as nature,

literal: yet in movement he kept within ritual bounds—that too was his mother's instruction.
idiomatic: yet he kept within ritual—his mother's teaching.
